listenings.text: Okay, voice note number one from Sao Paulo. I have been here for about five months now and I still cannot order coffee without pointing at something. My Portuguese is rusty in a way that is honestly embarrassing, because I studied it for a whole year before I came. But here is the thing nobody tells you about living abroad. You do not learn the language in a class. You pick it up in the gym, at the bus stop, standing in line at the bakery. I made three friends this month and every single one of them was somebody I met while I was doing something else. So my advice, if you are thinking about a year like this one: stop waiting until your language is good. It never gets good if you wait.

I have coached kids who stopped for two years and came back convinced they had lost everything. They had not. Here is what actually happens when you stop. The knowledge stays and the speed goes. You still know where to pass. You just take half a second longer to decide, and in a game half a second is everything. So the work is never relearning. The work is getting the decision back down to nothing. And that is good news, because rebuilding speed is a lot faster than building it the first time. The player who trained for four years and stopped for two is not a beginner. He is an athlete with rust on him, and rust comes off.

Here is a small experiment that travel writers love. Take somebody who has studied English for years, put them in an airport in another country, and watch. Almost nobody fails. They get by. They find the gate, they order the sandwich, they explain that a bag is missing. And then, on the plane home, the same person says the same sentence: my English is not good enough. What went wrong was not the English. What went wrong was the measurement. They compared themselves to a native speaker in a film, instead of to the only question that matters abroad, which is whether the other person understood and answered. By that measure most travelers pass every single day, and never once give themselves the point.
